\section{Introduction}
Douglas Hofstadter popularized the term \emph{strange loop} for a level structure
in which moving consistently upward (or downward) nevertheless returns one to one's
starting point. Escher's ascending staircases, self-referential sentences, and
self-drawing hands are the informal pictures; the phenomenon also sits at the
foundations of logic, where positing a single universe of types large enough to
contain itself leads directly to paradox.

This paper isolates the order-theoretic core of the strange-loop idea and proves,
in maximal simplicity, exactly when such loops can and cannot occur. The unifying
theme is a duality between \emph{loops} and \emph{levels}: a hierarchy admits
consistent numerical levels precisely when it is free of loops. When the two
collide, one must be surrendered; at the extreme, the maximal conceivable loop---a
universe reflecting its own totality of predicates---is self-contradictory by
Cantor's diagonal method.

We work with an arbitrary carrier type $\alpha$ and an arbitrary binary relation
$r:\alpha\to\alpha\to\mathrm{Prop}$, read as ``$r(x,y)$ means $x$ sits below $y$''
(equivalently, ``$x$ refers to $y$''). No transitivity, reflexivity, or antisymmetry
is assumed unless stated; the results depend only on the presence or absence of
two-cycles.

\section{Tangles and cycles}

\begin{definition}[Tangle]
A relation $r$ on $\alpha$ is \emph{tangled} if there exist $x,y\in\alpha$ with
$r(x,y)$ and $r(y,x)$. We write $\mathrm{IsTangled}(r):=\exists\,x\,y,\ r(x,y)\wedge r(y,x)$.
\end{definition}

This two-cycle is the minimal formal shape of a strange loop: each of $x,y$ lies
both above and below the other.

\begin{definition}[Self-loop]
A relation $r$ \emph{has a self-loop} if there exists $x$ with $r(x,x)$. This is the
degenerate one-element tangle.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
Every self-loop is a tangle.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Given $x$ with $r(x,x)$, take $y=x$; then $r(x,y)$ and $r(y,x)$ hold.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Asymmetry]
A relation $r$ is \emph{asymmetric} if for all $a,b$, $r(a,b)$ implies
$\neg\,r(b,a)$. This is the strict-order character of a hierarchy: no edge has a
reverse.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Asymmetry excludes tangles]\label{thm:asym}
If $r$ is asymmetric, then $r$ is not tangled.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $x,y$ satisfy $r(x,y)$ and $r(y,x)$. Asymmetry applied to $r(x,y)$ gives
$\neg\,r(y,x)$, contradicting $r(y,x)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tangles exclude asymmetry]
If $r$ is tangled, then $r$ is not asymmetric.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Contrapositive of Theorem~\ref{thm:asym}.
\end{proof}

Tangledness and asymmetry are thus exact opposites: to retain a strange loop is to
give up the strict-order character of a hierarchy.

\section{Well-founded hierarchies carry no tangle}

A relation $r$ is \emph{well-founded} if it admits no infinite descending chain;
equivalently, every nonempty subset has an $r$-minimal element. A standard
consequence is that a well-founded relation is asymmetric.

\begin{theorem}[Well-foundedness excludes tangles]\label{thm:wf}
If $r$ is well-founded, then $r$ is not tangled.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A well-founded relation is asymmetric; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:asym}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Strict orders are untangled]
For any preorder on $\alpha$, the strict relation $<$ is not tangled.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Strict order is asymmetric; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:asym}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The universe-level ladder is not tangled]\label{cor:ladder}
Modeling the tower $\mathrm{level}_0\prec\mathrm{level}_1\prec\cdots$ by
$(\mathbb{N},<)$, the relation $<$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is not tangled.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
$(\mathbb{N},<)$ is well-founded; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:wf}.
\end{proof}

The infinite cumulative hierarchy of type universes---each universe living strictly
inside the next---has the order type of $(\mathbb{N},<)$ and is therefore tangle-free.

\section{Grading: the price of a consistent tangle}

\begin{definition}[Grading]
A \emph{grading} of $r$ is a function $\rank:\alpha\to\mathbb{N}$ such that
$r(a,b)\Rightarrow\rank(a)<\rank(b)$ for all $a,b$: every edge strictly increases
rank.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Gradings forbid tangles]\label{thm:grade}
If $r$ admits a grading, then $r$ is not tangled.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $r(x,y)$ and $r(y,x)$, then $\rank(x)<\rank(y)$ and $\rank(y)<\rank(x)$, hence
$\rank(x)<\rank(x)$, impossible in $\mathbb{N}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Consistency dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
If $r$ is tangled, then $r$ admits no grading.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Contrapositive of Theorem~\ref{thm:grade}.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy} is the formal core of the principle that a
\emph{consistent} tangled hierarchy costs either consistency or the hierarchy: a
genuine tangle cannot be assigned consistent numerical levels. Retaining the loop
forces one to abandon the grading, and retaining the grading forces one to abandon
the loop.

\section{Apparent tangles from adjacency}

\begin{definition}[Adjacency]
Define $\refadj$ on $\mathbb{N}$ by $\refadj(n,m):=(m=n+1)\vee(n=m+1)$: a level may
refer to the level immediately above or below it. This models ``a term at level $n$
may mention level $n+1$'' on the reference graph.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacency is symmetric]
$\refadj(a,b)\Rightarrow\refadj(b,a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $b=a+1$ then the disjunct $a+1=b$ holds with roles swapped; symmetrically for
$a=b+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacency is tangled]\label{thm:adjtangled}
$\refadj$ is tangled.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take $x=0$, $y=1$: $\refadj(0,1)$ via $1=0+1$ and $\refadj(1,0)$ via $1=0+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry generates tangles]
If $r$ is symmetric and $r(x,y)$ holds for some $x,y$, then $r$ is tangled.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
From $r(x,y)$ and symmetry, $r(y,x)$; the pair $(x,y)$ witnesses the tangle.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Reference graphs are ungradable]
The adjacency relation admits no grading, even though it lives on top of the
well-founded ladder $(\mathbb{N},<)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
$\refadj$ is tangled (Theorem~\ref{thm:adjtangled}); apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy}.
\end{proof}

The tower of levels is untangled, but the graph of who may refer to whom is tangled
and ungradable: the strange loop is a phenomenon of cross-talk between levels, not
of the order on levels.

\section{The ultimate tangle: a self-reflecting universe is inconsistent}

\begin{theorem}[Diagonal / Cantor]\label{thm:cantor}
For any type $\alpha$ and any $f:\alpha\to\Pow(\alpha)$, $f$ is not surjective.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Consider $D=\{\,x\in\alpha:x\notin f(x)\,\}$. If $f$ were surjective there would be
$a$ with $f(a)=D$; then $a\in D\iff a\notin f(a)=D$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Reflective universe]
A \emph{reflective universe} on a type $U$ consists of a decoding
$\decode:U\to\Pow(U)$ together with a completeness condition: $\decode$ is
surjective. Each element $c$ names the subset $\decode(c)\subseteq U$ (a predicate
over $U$), and completeness says every predicate is named by some element of $U$.
This is the ultimate tangle: a universe reflecting its own power set, the shape of
``$\mathrm{Type}:\mathrm{Type}$.''
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The ultimate tangle is inconsistent]
No reflective universe exists: for every type $U$, the type of reflective universes
on $U$ is empty.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A reflective universe supplies a surjection $\decode:U\to\Pow(U)$, contradicting
Theorem~\ref{thm:cantor}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The Russell code]
Unwinding the proof, the offending element is the \emph{Russell code}: if $\decode$
were complete, some $a$ would name $R=\{\,x:x\notin\decode(x)\,\}$, and then
$a\in R\iff a\notin R$. The contradiction is exactly self-membership at equal
level. This is the Cantor/Russell/Girard core of the inconsistency of
``$\mathrm{Type}:\mathrm{Type}$.'' Consistent foundations therefore use the
infinite well-founded ladder of universes of Corollary~\ref{cor:ladder} rather than
a single self-containing universe.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}
Detecting whether a finite reference structure is tangled, and whether it admits a
grading, are decidable and efficient.

\begin{algorithm}[Two-cycle detection]
Given a finite relation as a directed graph $(V,E)$, check for each edge
$(x,y)\in E$ whether $(y,x)\in E$. This runs in $O(|E|)$ with a hash set of edges;
a positive answer returns the witnessing two-cycle.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Grading construction / obstruction]
A finite relation admits a grading iff its graph is acyclic. Run a topological sort:
if it succeeds, the topological index is a valid grading; if a cycle is found, it
certifies that no grading exists. This runs in $O(|V|+|E|)$;
Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy} is the two-cycle special case. Acyclicity, not merely
two-cycle freeness, is the exact condition for gradability.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Russell diagonal witness]
Given a finite universe $U$ and a decoding $\decode:U\to\Pow(U)$, construct
$R=\{\,x\in U:x\notin\decode(x)\,\}$ in $O(|U|)$ membership tests. Then $R$ is not
in the image of $\decode$, exhibiting an explicit unnamed predicate and
demonstrating incompleteness constructively.
\end{algorithm}

\section{Applications}
\textbf{Foundations of type theory.} The infinite hierarchy
$\mathrm{Type}_0:\mathrm{Type}_1:\cdots$ is untangled (Corollary~\ref{cor:ladder}),
while ``$\mathrm{Type}:\mathrm{Type}$'' is the inconsistent ultimate tangle.

\textbf{Citation and communication networks.} Symmetric reference relations are
tangled once they contain an edge, hence admit no consistent ranking unless
edgeless or oriented acyclically.

\textbf{Dependency and build systems.} A build graph compiles iff acyclic, i.e.
gradable; a circular dependency is a tangle, and topological sort returns either a
build order or the offending cycle.

\textbf{Self-reference and paradox.} The Russell code is the abstract engine behind
the liar paradox, Russell's paradox, Cantor's theorem, and Girard's paradox.

\section{Discussion}
The results center on the duality \emph{graded $\iff$ loop-free}. Well-foundedness
is the classical sufficient condition for loop-freeness; gradedness is a concrete
sufficient condition with a sharp obstruction; symmetry is a sufficient condition
for the presence of loops; and the diagonal argument shows the maximal loop is
outright contradictory. Keeping the tangle at its minimal two-cycle form makes
every proof short and axiom-light.

\section{Future Directions}
\textbf{Ordinal grading characterizes acyclicity.} We conjecture a relation admits
an ordinal rank strictly increasing along every edge iff it is well-founded;
replacing $\mathbb{N}$ by the ordinals should upgrade the dichotomy from two-cycles
to arbitrary loops.

\textbf{Longer loops cost more grading room.} We conjecture a relation with an
$n$-cycle but no shorter cycle admits a rank into $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ but into
no linearly ordered monoid; minimal cycle length is an exact ``how tangled''
invariant.

\textbf{Stratified reflection is the boundary of consistency.} We conjecture a
universe may consistently reflect all predicates of strictly lower rank but not its
own; the transition occurs exactly at the diagonal fixed point of the Russell code.

\textbf{Symmetric reference graphs are universally ungradable.} We conjecture any
symmetric reference relation with at least one edge is tangled, so only directed
acyclic reference structures can be graded.

    """Return a witnessing two-cycle (x, y) with x != y-order irrelevant,

    for (x, y) in edges:

    return None

    """True iff no edge has a reverse (the strict-order character)."""
    return all((y, x) not in edges for (x, y) in edges if x != y) and \

    topological sort), else None (a cycle -- a genuine tangle at some length --
    is present)."""
    verts = list(vertices)
    indeg = {v: 0 for v in verts}
    succ: dict = {v: [] for v in verts}
    for (a, b) in edges:
        succ[a].append(b)

    queue = [v for v in verts if indeg[v] == 0]

Tangled Hierarchies: Order, Grading, and the Ultimate Tangle
============================================================

Self-contained numerical demonstrations of the paper's results.

A relation r on a finite carrier is represented as a set of ordered pairs
(directed edges). We demonstrate:

  1. Tangle detection (two-cycles) and self-loops.
  2. Well-founded / strict orders (like (N, <)) carry no tangle.
  3. Grading forbids tangles; a tangle has no grading (consistency dichotomy).
  4. Adjacency (symmetric neighbour reference) is tangled though the order is not.
  5. The Russell diagonal witness: no decoding of a finite universe onto its
     power set can be surjective (the ultimate tangle is inconsistent).

Run:  python demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, FrozenSet, Iterable, Optional, Set, Tuple

Relation = Set[Tuple[int, int]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1 -- Tangles and cycles
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_tangled(edges: Relation) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Return a witnessing two-cycle (x, y) with x != y-order irrelevant,
    i.e. (x, y) and (y, x) both present, or None if the relation is untangled.
    Also detects self-loops (x, x)."""
    for (x, y) in edges:
        if (y, x) in edges:
            return (x, y)
    return None


def has_self_loop(edges: Relation) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return an x with (x, x) in the relation, else None."""
    for (x, y) in edges:
        if x == y:
            return x
    return None


def is_asymmetric(edges: Relation) -> bool:
    """True iff no edge has a reverse (the strict-order character)."""
    return all((y, x) not in edges for (x, y) in edges if x != y) and \
        has_self_loop(edges) is None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 2 & 3 -- Gradings and the consistency dichotomy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def find_grading(vertices: Iterable[int], edges: Relation) -> Optional[dict]:
    """Attempt to build a grading rank: V -> N with rank(a) < rank(b) for every
    edge (a, b). Returns the rank dict if the graph is acyclic (Kahn's
    topological sort), else None (a cycle -- a genuine tangle at some length --
    is present)."""
    verts = list(vertices)
    indeg = {v: 0 for v in verts}
    succ: dict = {v: [] for v in verts}
    for (a, b) in edges:
        succ[a].append(b)
        indeg[b] += 1
    queue = [v for v in verts if indeg[v] == 0]
    rank: dict = {}
    level = 0
    processed = 0
    while queue:
        nxt = []
        for v in queue:
            rank[v] = level
            processed += 1
            for w in succ[v]:
                indeg[w] -= 1
                if indeg[w] == 0:
                    nxt.append(w)
        queue = nxt
        level += 1
    if processed != len(verts):
        return None  # cycle detected: no grading exists
    return rank


def grading_is_valid(rank: dict, edges: Relation) -> bool:
    """Verify rank(a) < rank(b) for every edge."""
    return all(rank[a] < rank[b] for (a, b) in edges)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 4 -- Adjacency (polymorphic reference)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def refers_adjacent_edges(n_levels: int) -> Relation:
    """Symmetric adjacency on levels 0..n_levels-1: m = n+1 or n = m+1."""
    edges: Relation = set()
    for n in range(n_levels):
        for m in range(n_levels):
            if m == n + 1 or n == m + 1:
                edges.add((n, m))
    return edges


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 5 -- The Russell diagonal witness (ultimate tangle)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def russell_diagonal(
    universe: Iterable[int],
    decode: Callable[[int], FrozenSet[int]],
) -> FrozenSet[int]:
    """Given decode: U -> P(U), build the diagonal set
    R = { x in U : x not in decode(x) }, which is provably NOT decode(c) for
    any c, witnessing that no decoding is surjective."""
    return frozenset(x for x in universe if x not in decode(x))


def decode_is_surjective(
    universe: Iterable[int],
    decode: Callable[[int], FrozenSet[int]],
) -> bool:
    """Brute-force check whether decode hits every subset of the (small) universe."""
    U = list(universe)
    image = {decode(c) for c in U}
    # enumerate all subsets
    for bits in product([False, True], repeat=len(U)):
        subset = frozenset(u for u, b in zip(U, bits) if b)
        if subset not in image:
            return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Driver
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main() -> None:
    line = "=" * 68

    print(line)
    print("1. Tangles, self-loops, asymmetry")
    print(line)
    ladder = {(i, j) for i in range(5) for j in range(5) if i < j}  # (N,<) up to 5
    print("Strict order < on {0..4}: tangled? ", is_tangled(ladder),
          "| asymmetric?", is_asymmetric(ladder))
    two_cycle = {(0, 1), (1, 0)}
    print("Two-cycle {0<->1}:          tangled? ", is_tangled(two_cycle),
          "| asymmetric?", is_asymmetric(two_cycle))
    self_loop = {(3, 3)}
    print("Self-loop {3->3}:           tangled? ", is_tangled(self_loop),
          "| self-loop at", has_self_loop(self_loop))

    print()
    print(line)
    print("2 & 3. Grading and the consistency dichotomy")
    print(line)
    V = list(range(5))
    g = find_grading(V, ladder)
    print("Grading of (N,<) ladder:", g, "-> valid?", grading_is_valid(g, ladder))
    g2 = find_grading([0, 1], two_cycle)
    print("Grading of two-cycle:   ", g2, "(None => tangle admits NO grading)")

    print()
    print(line)
    print("4. Adjacency is tangled though the level order is not")
    print(line)
    adj = refers_adjacent_edges(6)
    print("Adjacency on levels 0..5: tangled witness =", is_tangled(adj))
    print("Adjacency grading:", find_grading(list(range(6)), adj),
          "(None => symmetric reference graph is ungradable)")

    print()
    print(line)
    print("5. The Russell diagonal witness -- no reflective universe")
    print(line)
    universe = [0, 1, 2]

    # A concrete (arbitrary) attempted decoding U -> P(U):
    table = {
        0: frozenset({0, 1}),
        1: frozenset({2}),
        2: frozenset({0, 1, 2}),
    }
    decode = lambda c: table[c]
    R = russell_diagonal(universe, decode)
    print("Universe:", universe)
    print("decode:  ", {c: set(table[c]) for c in universe})
    print("Russell diagonal R = { x : x not in decode(x) } =", set(R))
    named = [c for c in universe if decode(c) == R]
    print("Codes naming R:", named, "(empty => R is unnamed, decode not onto)")
    print("Is decode surjective onto P(U)?", decode_is_surjective(universe, decode))

    # Try EVERY possible decoding of a 2-element universe; none is surjective.
    print()
    print("Exhaustive check: no decoding of a 2-element universe is surjective")

            if decode_is_surjective(U2, lambda c: d[c]):
                found_surjective = True
    print("Any surjective decoding found?", found_surjective,
          "(False => the ultimate tangle is impossible)")

    main()

+theorem consistency_not_internally_provable (w : F.World) (hw : ∃ v, F.R w v) :
+    w ∉ F.boxSet F.Con := by
+  obtain ⟨ v, hv ⟩ := hw;
+  -- By `godel_second`, if `w` were in `F.boxSet F.Con`, then `w` would also be in `F.boxSet ∅`.
+  intro h
+  apply F.godel_second h v hv
+
+/-
+A **self-sound** (reflective) world for the false proposition is automatically
+consistent: if `□⊥ → ⊥` holds at `w`, then `w` has a successor.
+-/
+theorem soundness_forces_consistency (w : F.World)
+    (hsound : w ∈ F.boxSet (∅ : Set F.World) → w ∈ (∅ : Set F.World)) :
+    w ∈ F.Con := by
+  contrapose! hsound; simp_all +decide [ GLFrame.boxSet ] ;
+  exact fun v hv => hsound ⟨ v, hv ⟩
+
+end GLFrame
+
+/-! ## The diagonal / fixed-point core of self-reference -/
+
+/-
+**Lawvere's fixed-point theorem.** If some map `f : A → (A → B)` is point-surjective
+(every `A → B` is `f a` for some `a`), then every endomap `g : B → B` has a fixed point.
+This is the categorical engine behind every diagonal/self-reference argument.
+-/
+theorem lawvere_fixed_point {A B : Type*} (f : A → (A → B))
+    (hf : Function.Surjective f) (g : B → B) : ∃ b, g b = b := by
+  obtain ⟨ a, ha ⟩ := hf ( fun a => g ( f a a ) );
+  exact ⟨ _, congr_fun ha a |> Eq.symm ⟩
+
+/-
+**Tarski undefinability / Cantor.** No proof system can carry a surjective
+self-encoding onto its own `Bool`-valued predicates: there is no point-surjective
+`f : A → (A → Bool)`, because `Bool.not` is a fixed-point-free endomap.
+-/
+theorem cantor_no_truth_predicate {A : Type*} :
+    ¬ ∃ f : A → (A → Bool), Function.Surjective f := by
+  by_contra h
+  obtain ⟨f, hf⟩ := h;
+  exact absurd ( @lawvere_fixed_point A Bool f hf Bool.not ) ( by simp +decide )
+
+/-! ## A concrete infinite Gödel–Löb frame -/
+
+/-
+The natural numbers with "accessible = strictly smaller" form a genuine infinite
+Gödel–Löb frame: transitive and converse well-founded.
+-/
+def natFrame : GLFrame where
+  World := ℕ
+  R := fun a b => b < a
+  trans' := fun hab hbc => lt_trans hbc hab
+  wf := by
+    exact wellFounded_lt
+
+/-
+In `natFrame`, world `0` has no successor: it vacuously proves everything (a dead,
+inconsistent theory) and is *not* consistent.
+-/
+theorem natFrame_zero_dead : (0 : ℕ) ∉ natFrame.Con := by
+  exact fun h => by obtain ⟨ v, hv ⟩ := h; exact Nat.not_lt_zero v hv;
+
+/-
+In `natFrame`, every nonzero world is consistent (has a successor) and therefore,
+by the tangled-hierarchy theorem, cannot prove its own consistency.
+-/
+theorem natFrame_succ_consistent (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) :
+    n ∈ natFrame.Con ∧ n ∉ natFrame.boxSet natFrame.Con := by
+  constructor;
+  · exact ⟨ _, hn ⟩;
+  · convert TangledHierarchies.GLFrame.consistency_not_internally_provable natFrame n ⟨ 0, hn ⟩ using 1
+
+/-- Example instantiation of the fixed-point core. -/
+example (g : Bool → Bool) (f : ℕ → (ℕ → Bool)) (hf : Function.Surjective f) :
+    ∃ b, g b = b := lawvere_fixed_point f hf g
+
+#check @GLFrame.semantic_loeb
+#check @GLFrame.godel_second
+#check @GLFrame.consistency_not_internally_provable
+#check @lawvere_fixed_point
+
+end TangledHierarchies

# Computational Evidence — Alien Number Systems

Concise numerical support for the two formalized systems: **base `-2`** (negabinary)
and **base `φ`** (the golden-ratio system).

## 1. Negabinary (base `-2`)

Value of a bit list, least-significant bit first: `value = Σ dᵢ·(-2)ⁱ`.
Canonical form = no trailing `0` (list does not end in `false`).

| n  | canonical bits (LSB→MSB) | standard "digit string" | check |
|----|--------------------------|-------------------------|-------|
| 0  | `[]`                     | `0`                     | 0 |
| 1  | `[1]`                    | `1`                     | 1 |
| 2  | `[0,1,1]`                | `110`                   | 0 − 2 + 4 = 2 |
| 3  | `[1,1,1]`                | `111`                   | 1 − 2 + 4 = 3 |
| 4  | `[0,0,1]`                | `100`                   | 4 = 4 |
| −1 | `[1,1]`                  | `11`                    | 1 − 2 = −1 |
| −2 | `[0,1]`                  | `10`                    | 0 − 2 = −2 |
| −3 | `[1,0,1,1]`              | `1101`                  | 1 + 0 + 4 − 8 = −3 |

**Observations.**
* Both positive and negative integers appear with digits `{0,1}` only — no sign.
* Every integer in the sample has exactly one canonical representation, matching the
  proved bijection `negabinary_unique_rep`.
* **Counterexample hunt (uniqueness).** Dropping canonicality breaks uniqueness:
  `[]`, `[0]`, `[0,0]` all evaluate to `0`. This is why the "no trailing `0`"
  condition is mandatory; the proof `nvalue_eq_zero_of_canonical` isolates exactly
  this failure mode.
* **OEIS.** Negabinary representations of `0,1,2,…` are catalogued as A039724.

## 2. Base `φ` (golden-ratio system)

`φ = (1+√5)/2`, `φ² = φ + 1`, and `φ⁻² = 2 − φ`.

Phinary expansions (digit strings, radix point separating non-negative and negative
exponents):

| n | base-`φ` string | powers used | check |
|---|-----------------|-------------|-------|
| 1 | `1`        | φ⁰               | 1 |
| 2 | `10.01`    | φ¹ + φ⁻²         | φ + (2−φ) = 2 |
| 3 | `100.01`   | φ² + φ⁻²         | (φ+1) + (2−φ) = 3 |
| 4 | `101.01`   | φ² + φ⁰ + φ⁻²    | (φ+1) + 1 + (2−φ) = 4 |

**Observations.**
* No expansion contains two consecutive `1`s — the positional shadow of the collapse
  rule `φⁿ + φⁿ⁺¹ = φⁿ⁺²` (formalized as `phiPow_carry`, i.e. `011 = 100`).
* Values with only non-negative exponents always lie in `ℤ + ℤ·φ` with Fibonacci
  coordinates (`phiSum_fib`); genuine integers require the symmetric ± exponent
  pattern (`phi_repr_three` gives `3 = φ² + φ⁻²`).
* Coordinate uniqueness of `a·φ + b` over `ℚ` is a consequence of the irrationality
  of `φ` (`phi_coord_unique`) — over `ℝ` it would fail.

# Future Directions — Alien Number Systems

Bold, falsifiable conjectures distilled from this cycle's study of negative,
complex, and irrational bases.

## 1. A uniform bijection theorem for every base `b ≤ -2`

**Conjecture.** For every integer base `b ≤ -2`, the map sending a canonical digit
string (digits in `{0,1,…,|b|-1}`, no trailing zero) to its value is a bijection
onto all of `ℤ`.

*The key insight is* that the entire argument for base `-2` rested on two
base-agnostic facts: the least-significant digit is pinned down by the residue of
the value modulo `|b|`, and a single interleaving measure on `ℤ` strictly decreases
under the base-`b` successor step. Neither fact used `b = -2` in any essential way.

*Why now?* The base-`-2` case is now settled with a fully explicit, self-contained
proof whose only base-specific input is the termination measure; generalizing the
measure to arbitrary negative `b` is the natural and immediate next step.

## 2. Gaussian integers in base `i − 1`

**Conjecture.** Every Gaussian integer has a unique representation in base `i − 1`
using the binary digits `{0,1}`, mirroring the negabinary bijection but over `ℤ[i]`
instead of `ℤ`.

*The key insight is* that `(i-1)` has norm `2`, so reduction modulo `i-1` leaves
exactly the two residues `{0,1}`; the same "residue fixes the next digit, quotient
shrinks" recursion should carry over verbatim once the interleaving measure on `ℤ`
is replaced by the complex norm.

*Why now?* The negabinary proof is structured precisely as "residue + shrinking
measure", a template that transplants to any Euclidean-like base; base `i-1` is the
smallest genuinely two-dimensional test of that template.

## 3. Base `φ` is the unique irrational base with the no-consecutive-digit law

**Conjecture.** Among real bases `β > 1`, the golden ratio is the *only* one for
which the greedy digit expansion of every real in `[0,1)` avoids the pattern `11`
while using digits `{0,1}`; equivalently, `β = φ` is forced by demanding that the
collapse identity `βⁿ + βⁿ⁺¹ = βⁿ⁺²` hold.

*The key insight is* that the collapse identity is literally `β² = β + 1`, whose only
root greater than `1` is `φ`; the no-consecutive-`1`s phenomenon is therefore not a
lucky feature of `φ` but its defining algebraic signature.

*Why now?* We have already isolated the collapse rule `φⁿ + φⁿ⁺¹ = φⁿ⁺²` as the sole
engine behind the digit restriction, turning a qualitative folklore statement into a
precise uniqueness claim about roots of `X² − X − 1`.

## 4. Fibonacci-coordinate integrality criterion in base `φ`

**Conjecture.** A finite base-`φ` value with non-negative exponents, `Σ_{i∈S} φⁱ`, is
an integer if and only if the Fibonacci coordinate `Σ_{i∈S} F_i` (the coefficient of
`φ`) vanishes; and the only way to realize a nonzero integer with digits `{0,1}` is
to admit negative exponents in a symmetric (Lucas) pattern.

*The key insight is* that every such value lands in `ℤ + ℤ·φ` with coordinates that
are Fibonacci sums, and irrationality of `φ` forces the `φ`-coordinate to be `0` for
the value to be rational.

*Why now?* Both halves of the mechanism are already in hand — the Fibonacci-sum
coordinate formula and coordinate uniqueness from irrationality — so the criterion
is a direct synthesis waiting to be proved.

## 5. A base tuned to prime patterns

**Conjecture.** There is no integer base `b` in which the set of primes is eventually
periodic in its least-significant digits beyond the constraints already imposed by
residues modulo small numbers; any "Ulam-spiral-like" regularity of primes in a base
`b` is fully explained by coprimality to `b`, not by the base itself.

*The key insight is* that a base only reorganizes residue information already present
in `ℤ/bℤ`, so genuine new prime structure cannot be manufactured by a change of
radix — the apparent patterns are shadows of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in
arithmetic progressions.

*Why now?* Framing the "alien prime base" dream as a rigorous non-existence statement
converts a vague search into a testable claim about residue classes, sharply focusing
where (if anywhere) real structure could hide.
